answers.answer: A caller supplies a key identifying an entry and gets its associated value. Use a settings namespace and a key encoding tenant ID and device ID with a separator disallowed in either ID (or consistently escaped); for example tenant-9|device-7 in settings, with every caller using the same encoding. The separate status namespace avoids confusing status with settings. Store the complete settings record as the value because those fields are read together. This is authoritative because the application treats it as the source of truth; caching would mean a disposable copy held elsewhere. The access model does not guarantee crash survival; verify persistence and failure guarantees. Replacement put first stores {mode: quiet, color: green}, then replaces it with {mode: loud}; get returns {mode: loud}, with color gone. Delete removes the entry; a get observing that deletion confirms absence. A get timeout means no result arrived, so existence is unknown and it must not be treated as not found. Knowing or guessing the key is not authorization: check access to this tenant and record before reading or writing.

evidence.quote: A key-value store can hold authoritative data, the record the application treats as its source of truth.
The key-value label says nothing by itself about whether acknowledged writes survive a crash.
In a replacement API, putting {mode: quiet, color: green}, then {mode: loud}, leaves only {mode: loud}. The old color field is gone.
A get timeout means no result arrived. It does not tell you whether the key exists.
A separator is safe only if values cannot contain it or are escaped consistently.
Verify the caller's access to the organization and record before reading or changing it.

answers.answer: A lookup needs a known equipment ID; having region inside the value does not supply matching IDs. A scan examines entries and filters for west, with read work growing with entries inspected even when few match. A region-to-IDs index maintains another lookup: obtain west candidate IDs and then fetch needed records without inspecting every value. It adds storage and update work: when equipment changes region or is deleted, corresponding index entries must change. Verify who maintains it and when results reflect writes; an application-maintained index requires coordination. Basic key-value access does not promise an index, so check the chosen store.

evidence.quote: Storing the city inside each value does not create an efficient lookup by city.
Its work grows with the entries inspected, even if few match.
It can find candidates without inspecting every value, then fetch the needed records.
When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too.
Some stores supply indexes or ordered range queries; basic key-value access promises neither.

answers.answer: Both blind writes store 21, leaving 21 rather than 22: one intended increment is lost. With the conditional operation, one worker tests version 7 and writes 21 plus an advanced version as one indivisible operation. The other worker still supplies version 7; it no longer matches, so its stale write is rejected. It rereads 21 and the current version, recomputes 22 and conditionally writes against that version, which succeeds if no intervening change occurs. Bound further retries under contention. A separate version check and unconditional put leave a gap in which another worker can change the value; both workers can pass the check before either writes. The condition and mutation must be atomic together.

evidence.quote: Both writes can succeed, but the final count is 11 instead of 12. One intended increment is lost.
Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation.
The rejected caller rereads the current value and version, recomputes its change and makes another conditional attempt.
Checking the version in a separate request before an unconditional put leaves the same race.

answers.answer: A timeout leaves execution unknown: the write may have completed and its response been lost. Repeating an identical replacement leaves the same result if no other write intervenes. Retrying an increment adds again if the first executed, even if each increment is atomic. Prevent this by recognizing the same logical operation with the same ID and intent on retries, atomically coordinating duplicate recording and the data change, and retaining duplicate records for the retry window. Verify actual product support and its scope; an ID alone is insufficient. Without verified duplicate protection, reconcile via an application recovery path instead of blindly repeating the increment; the lesson does not specify that recovery implementation. Use bounded retries/backoff for retryable failures. TTL triggers expiration; eviction removes entries to manage capacity under the configured policy. Eviction can happen before TTL, so TTL does not promise retention. Neither refreshes data; a cache may reload its source, whereas authoritative data needs retention/recovery policy. TTL does not schedule an exact-time business action: enforce access deadlines when authorizing use and use a suitable work-execution mechanism for timed actions. Check TTL support, when expired data stops being returned versus physical deletion, eviction configuration, replacement semantics, and retry/duplicate guarantees in the selected product.

evidence.quote: A write can finish and its reply can be lost.
Replacing a value with the identical value twice does this if no other write intervenes.
Executing an increment twice adds twice, even if each increment is individually atomic.
A request ID alone is insufficient: recording it and changing the data must be coordinated atomically, with duplicate records retained for the retry window.
An entry can disappear before its TTL; a TTL is not a promise to retain it until the deadline.
Neither removal mechanism fetches a fresh replacement.
Expiration is also not a scheduler promising that business work runs at the exact deadline.
Check TTL support, expiry visibility and eviction configuration in the chosen implementation before relying on any of them.

answers.answer: A partition is a portion of the keyspace assigned to a node or group. Assigning different key groups to different serving resources spreads storage and request work for many-key workloads. A hot key receives disproportionate traffic; adding partitions may leave that key limited by the same serving capacity. Measure requests across keys, not just key counts. An older value from a lagging maintained copy concerns read consistency: the selected read mode may allow stale results after an acknowledged write. Durability concerns survival of acknowledged data through specified failures; a durable write may not yet appear in a lagging read, and seeing the latest value does not establish crash survival. Before promising freshness or survival, check the implementation, persistence and replication settings, selected read/write modes, which writes reads must observe, and the failures acknowledged writes survive. More nodes or acknowledgement alone cannot establish these promises.

evidence.quote: A portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group.
More partitions alone may not help when most work still targets that key's serving capacity.
if it lags and the read mode permits stale results, it can return an older value after a successful write.
A durable write can still be absent from a lagging read. Conversely, seeing a new value does not prove that it will survive a crash.
Check the implementation, persistence and replication settings, and the selected read/write mode.

answers.answer: A fits directly: its known account key selects the independent preferences record for retrieval or replacement without a scan to discover matches. B needs more than basic key lookup: changing filters may require scans that read extra entries or indexes with ongoing update work, and application-side joins add requests and coordination. Richer query or transaction support may fit B better. For A I would verify atomic conditional updates if simultaneous preference edits must not overwrite each other: read-then-replace leaves a race and stale replacement can lose another change. I would also verify traffic distribution and hot-key serving capacity, because a disproportionately popular account can remain a bottleneck despite many partitions. The model alone does not establish speed or safety; verify required guarantees and measure representative requests and failures, including behavior when unavailable. Network, value size and implementation limits also affect performance.

evidence.quote: Independent records fetched and replaced by a known key are a direct fit.
Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.
The condition and the write must share the same atomic boundary.
Measure the distribution of requests, not just the number of keys.
Measure representative requests and failures.
network, value size, hot keys and implementation limits still affect latency and capacity.
